cases.n: Archdiocese of Paderborn — University of Paderborn study (2026)
cases.who: Catholic Archdiocese of Paderborn; archbishops Lorenz Jaeger and Johannes Joachim Degenhardt
cases.cover: The study found sexual violence against children was concealed over decades; the tenures of Cardinals Jaeger and Degenhardt were assessed critically.
cases.d: Historians at the University of Paderborn, commissioned by the archdiocese, published their study on 12 March 2026. It identified 210 accused people and 489 victims and found that sexual violence against children was concealed for decades under Archbishops Lorenz Jaeger and Johannes Joachim Degenhardt. Paderborn city council then voted to rename streets named after both cardinals and to remove them from its honorary citizens. In September 2026 the archdiocese's independent review commission reported 262 accused clergy and church employees known by the end of June 2026.
cases.cite: Universität Paderborn, historical study of sexual abuse in the Archdiocese of Paderborn 1941–2002, 12 March 2026 (epd via evangelisch.de, 26 March 2026); Unabhängige Aufarbeitungskommission Paderborn, fourth annual report (epd, 4 September 2026)

cases.n: Diocese of Passau — University of Passau study (2025)
cases.victims_note: at least 672 minors sexually abused or physically mistreated by clergy; authors think the real number may be double
cases.who: Catholic Diocese of Passau — priests, deacons and religious brothers
cases.cover: Bishops and vicars general often put protecting the institution and the priesthood above victims; judges, prosecutors, medical experts and school and youth authorities are named as bystanders.
cases.d: A University of Passau team led by historian Marc von Knorring, commissioned by the diocese's independent review commission, published its study in December 2025 covering 1945 to 2022. It found at least 672 minors, mostly boys, abused by 154 clergy (about 6.4% of some 2,400 clergy in the period), 128 of whom sexually abused minors; about 86% were likely repeat offenders. Abuse took place in boarding schools and homes, religious lessons and altar-server duties. The study found bishops and vicars general often protected the institution rather than victims.
cases.cite: Marc von Knorring and team, Universität Passau, study for the Unabhängige Aufarbeitungskommission of the Diocese of Passau, December 2025 (ZDFheute)

cases.n: Diocese of Würzburg — Schneider report for the review commission (2025)
cases.who: Catholic Diocese of Würzburg (43 of 51 accused were clergy)
cases.cover: Until the early 2000s some accused clergy received 'systematic protection'.
cases.d: Lawyer Hendrik Schneider, commissioned by the diocese's independent review commission (UKAM), presented his report on 8 April 2025 covering 1949 to 2019. It counted 51 accused, 43 of them clergy, and 226 victims subject to 449 documented acts, which the report extrapolated to about 3,053 acts. The average age at the first act was 9.8 years. It found systematic protection of some accused clergy until the early 2000s. Earlier reviews of all personnel files (Schrepfer law firm, 2019) and of the three Kilianeen boarding schools (2019) preceded it.
cases.cite: Hendrik Schneider, report for the Unabhängige Kommission zur Aufarbeitung des sexuellen Missbrauchs im Bistum Würzburg, 8 April 2025 (epd via evangelisch.de)

cases.n: Diocese of Hildesheim — Niewisch-Lennartz expert group on the Janssen era (2021)
cases.who: Catholic Diocese of Hildesheim under Bishop Heinrich Maria Janssen
cases.cover: Priests accused of abusing children were generally only moved to another parish; perpetrators got support and protection while victims got no help.
cases.d: An external expert group chaired by former Lower Saxony justice minister Antje Niewisch-Lennartz presented its report on 14 September 2021 on the tenure of Bishop Heinrich Maria Janssen (1957–1982). It identified 71 suspects, 45 clergy and 26 lay staff, 51 of them from Janssen's tenure. Accused priests were generally only transferred, and children were left unprotected in tent camps, priests' homes and church children's homes. The group found no further evidence against Janssen himself but did not refute two allegations made against him in 2015 and 2018. An earlier IPP study for the diocese appeared in 2017.
cases.cite: Antje Niewisch-Lennartz, Kurt Schrimm and IPP, report for the Diocese of Hildesheim, 14 September 2021 (LTO)

cases.n: Diocese of Augsburg — independent review commission study (2025)
cases.who: Catholic Diocese of Augsburg; bishops and vicars general 1949–2019
cases.cover: Diocesan leaders did not respond appropriately to allegations for decades: share of inappropriate handling 54.5% under Freundorfer, 63.6% under Stimpfle, 68.8% under Dammertz, 33.3% under Mixa, 5.9% under Zdarsa.
cases.d: The diocese's independent review commission (UAKA) presented a 206-page study on 30 October 2025, built on the diocese's MHG study files of 1,507 clergy. It found 77 accused linked to 193 offences against 156 victims, about two-thirds male and 42.5% under 14, with offences back to 1948. Diocesan leaders handled allegations inappropriately for decades, in up to 68.8% of cases under one bishop; handling improved after the 2002 guidelines. Separate studies covered the Catholic children's homes Heilig Kreuz (Donauwörth) and Reitenbuch.
cases.cite: Unabhängige Aufarbeitungskommission des Bistums Augsburg (UAKA), study presented 30 October 2025 (epd via Sonntagsblatt)

cases.n: Diocese of Fulda — independent review commission final report (2025)
cases.victims_note: 120 identified; the commission says the true total is several times higher
cases.who: Catholic Diocese of Fulda; auxiliary bishop Johannes Kapp (personnel chief 1977–2003)
cases.cover: Until about 2000 accused clergy were treated leniently to protect the church's reputation and transferred without stated reasons; victims were ignored until 2010.
cases.d: The independent commission for the Diocese of Fulda, chaired by former Fulda mayor Gerhard Möller, presented its final report in June 2025 after reviewing 2,124 files covering about 80 years. It identified 120 victims and 37 accused priests and chaplains, with 239 provable sexual offences. Until about 2000 accused clergy were treated leniently and moved without explanation, and victims were ignored until 2010; auxiliary bishop Johannes Kapp, in charge of personnel from 1977 to 2003, was named as mainly responsible. Bishop Michael Gerber said the report showed systematic failure.
cases.cite: Unabhängige Kommission zur Aufarbeitung sexualisierter Gewalt im Bistum Fulda, final report, June 2025 (epd via evangelisch.de, 17 June 2025)

cases.n: Diocese of Speyer — University of Mannheim study, part 1 (2025)
cases.who: Catholic Diocese of Speyer; religious orders working in it
cases.cover: Accused priests were either punished individually or protected; structural problems, including weak oversight of religious orders, were ignored.
cases.d: Historian Sylvia Schraut of the University of Mannheim, in a study begun in 2023 at the initiative of the diocese's independent review commission, presented part 1 in May 2025. It identified 109 accused clergy since 1946; half the cases were in the 1950s and 1960s, in church homes and schools, confession and parish work. The church either punished accused priests individually or shielded them, and oversight of religious orders was weak. Part 2, with case analyses, is due in 2027. Separately, in 2020 a social court granted victim compensation to a man abused in the former children's home of the Niederbronn Sisters in Speyer, where he and two other men said nuns brought children to abusers in 1963–1975.
cases.cite: Sylvia Schraut, 'Sexueller Missbrauch im Bistum Speyer seit 1946 – Teilstudie 1', Universität Mannheim, press release 8 May 2025; epd report on the Engelsgasse children's home, 11 December 2020

cases.n: Diocese of Limburg — 'Betroffene hören – Missbrauch verhindern' project (2020)
cases.who: Catholic Diocese of Limburg; bishops, vicars general and personnel directors
cases.cover: The file review named diocesan leaders responsible for 'cover-up and silence' and found that protecting the institution guided decisions.
cases.d: The Diocese of Limburg ran a project with about 70 mostly external experts from September 2019 to June 2020 as its response to the 2018 MHG study; the 415-page final report was presented on 13 June 2020 in Frankfurt's Paulskirche. Its file review covered 46 cases of accused clergy and found that diocesan leaders had played down the crimes and treated the accused as a risk to the clerical system rather than a danger to children. It named the responsible leaders and produced 61 measures against abuse. Few victims came forward to the project.
cases.cite: Bistum Limburg, 'Betroffene hören – Missbrauch verhindern. Konsequenzen aus der MHG-Studie', final report, 13 June 2020

cases.n: Archdiocese of Hamburg — University of Ulm study of abuse in Mecklenburg 1946–1989 (2023)
cases.who: Catholic Church in Mecklenburg (Archdiocese of Hamburg); East German Ministry for State Security (Stasi)
cases.cover: The Stasi recruited suspects as informers, so no prosecutions followed; church leaders knew, and church–state arrangements such as moving suspects to West Germany kept cases quiet.
cases.d: Forensic psychiatrists at the University of Ulm led by Manuela Dudeck, commissioned by the Archdiocese of Hamburg, presented their study in Schwerin on 24 February 2023. Reviewing 1,503 church and Stasi files, they identified 19 suspects and 40 victims, on average about 10 years old. Parishes and church leaders knew of abuse, and the study found a culture of silence and partly active cover-up. The Stasi recruited suspects as informers and used them, so prosecutions did not follow, and suspects were moved to West Germany.
cases.cite: Manuela Dudeck and Laura Rinser, Universität Ulm, study for the Archdiocese of Hamburg, 24 February 2023 (epd via evangelisch.de)

cases.n: Salesians of Don Bosco, German Province — working group report (2011)
cases.victims_note: 120 complaints; about half concern sexual abuse, half physical violence
cases.who: Salesians of Don Bosco, German Province — homes and schools
cases.d: A working group with internal and external members set up by the German Province of the Salesians of Don Bosco reported on 23 February 2011. It had received 120 complaints concerning Salesian facilities from 1950 into the 1980s, about half about sexual abuse and half about physical violence, against members of the order and employees. About two-thirds of the cases had been clarified, and cases were referred to prosecutors.
cases.cite: Salesianer Don Boscos, Deutsche Provinz, Arbeitsgruppe zur Aufklärung von Misshandlungs- und Missbrauchsfällen, report of 23 February 2011

cases.n: German Capuchin Province — Westpfahl Spilker Wastl report (2011)
cases.victims_note: at least 11 of the accused friars are believed to have abused minors; no total victim count
cases.who: Capuchin Order, German Province (former Bavarian and Rhine-Westphalian provinces); Burghausen seminary
cases.cover: Personnel files of dead friars appear to have been 'cleaned'; no canonical investigation was opened in any case; suspects were quietly reassigned and only one case reached prosecutors.
cases.d: Lawyer Martin Pusch of Westpfahl Spilker Wastl, commissioned by the German Capuchin provincial, reported on 30 November 2011. He found 32 accused friars, 19 of them accused of sexual abuse and at least 11 believed to have abused minors, mostly in schools and training institutions including the Burghausen seminary. Files of deceased friars appeared to have been purged, no church-law investigation was opened in any case, and suspects were quietly reassigned. Before 2010 victims received little or no support.
cases.cite: Martin Pusch (Westpfahl Spilker Wastl), report for the Provincial of the German Capuchin Province, 30 November 2011

cases.n: Redemptorists in Germany — interim reports (2010–2024) and IPP study (2026)
cases.victims_note: at least 90, mostly pupils
cases.who: Redemptorist order in Germany — schools including the Collegium Josephinum, Bonn
cases.d: Between 2010 and 2024 the Redemptorist order in Germany commissioned six interim reports on sexual violence, mainly at its schools. They documented at least 90 victims, mostly pupils, and at least 29 perpetrators from 1950 to 2011, including at the order's Collegium Josephinum grammar school in Bonn. In September 2026 the order presented a 276-page study by the Munich IPP institute (Heiner Keupp), commissioned jointly with survivors, on how it handled the cases from 2010.
cases.cite: Redemptorist order, interim reports 2010–2024; IPP München (Heiner Keupp), study presented in Bonn, September 2026 (epd via evangelisch.de, 25 September 2026)

cases.n: Franciscan Minorites (German province) — independent study (2024)
cases.victims_note: one friar alone abused 20 people; many victims were children in the order's boarding schools in Bonn and Würzburg
cases.who: Order of Friars Minor Conventual (Minorites), German province
cases.cover: Some accused abused for almost 30 years before sanctions took hold; threatened consequences were not enforced across changes of superiors.
cases.d: Lawyers Petra Ladenburger and Martina Lörsch presented a 152-page study on 10 June 2024, the first independent externally supervised study of a Catholic order in Germany under the 2021 agreement between the orders' conference (DOK) and the federal abuse commissioner. It assessed allegations against nine friars since the 1960s; one friar's case involved 20 people, and many victims were children in the order's boarding schools in Bonn and Würzburg. Some accused abused for nearly 30 years before effective sanctions, because successive superiors did not enforce consequences.
cases.cite: Petra Ladenburger and Martina Lörsch, study for the German Province of the Franciscan Minorites, 10 June 2024 (Vatican News)

cases.n: German Franciscan Province — IPP study (2026)
cases.victims_note: more than 100, mostly minors; about 75% male; 'tip of the iceberg'
cases.who: German Franciscan Province (OFM) — educational institutions incl. Vossenack school and boarding school
cases.d: The Munich IPP institute, led by Peter Caspari, presented its study for the German Franciscan Province on 25 February 2026, covering the period since 1945. It identified more than 100 victims, mostly minors aged 10 to 15 when the abuse began and about three-quarters male, and 98 suspected perpetrators; most abuse took place in educational institutions. The provincial minister acknowledged structural problems and the order's guilt. A survivor from the Vossenack school accused the leadership of years of cover-up.
cases.cite: IPP München (Peter Caspari), study for the Deutsche Franziskanerprovinz, 25 February 2026 (epd via evangelisch.de)

cases.n: Aloisiuskolleg Bonn (Jesuit school) — Zinsmeister report (2011)
cases.victims_note: 58 reports of abuse and other violations; authors said far from complete
cases.who: Society of Jesus — Aloisiuskolleg boarding school, Bonn
cases.cover: A priest responsible for more than half the reports, later rector, was never stopped.
cases.d: An independent team led by Cologne law professor Julia Zinsmeister presented its report on the Jesuit Aloisiuskolleg on 15 February 2011, covering about 60 years. It received 58 reports of abuse and other violations against 23 staff, 18 Jesuit priests and 5 lay employees, most active in the 1950s and 1960s. Ten cases concerned the former headmaster, who led and lived at the school from 1968 to 2008, and would count as sexual abuse under strict criminal-law standards. The authors blamed the order's closed organisational culture.
cases.cite: Julia Zinsmeister et al., final report on the Aloisiuskolleg, 15 February 2011 (epd via evangelisch.de)

cases.n: Collegium Josephinum, Bad Münstereifel — Archdiocese of Cologne project report (2017)
cases.victims_note: about 100 former pupils gave accounts; no total victim count
cases.who: Archdiocese of Cologne — Collegium Josephinum boarding school (closed 1997)
cases.cover: The archdiocese, as operator, set no rules for educational methods and did not monitor practice.
cases.d: A project led by educational scientist Claudia Bundschuh, with Bettina Janssen as operational lead and commissioned by the Archdiocese of Cologne, published its final report on 13 September 2017. About 100 former pupils described violence at the boarding school from at least the 1950s; the report found a 'system of abuse of power' up to at least the 1970s. Seven staff, all but one priests, were accused of sexual violence and twelve of physical violence. The archdiocese set no rules and did not supervise the school.
cases.cite: Claudia Bundschuh, Bettina Janssen and Arnfried Bintig, final report on the Collegium Josephinum Bad Münstereifel, 13 September 2017 (Archdiocese of Cologne press release via domradio.de)

cases.n: Albertinum Gerolstein — Diocese of Trier boarding school report (2022)
cases.victims_note: 54 former pupils came forward
cases.who: Diocese of Trier — Bischöfliches Internat Albertinum, Gerolstein; its three priest-directors
cases.cover: The diocese lacked effective oversight; pupils who reported beatings were not believed and survivors received no help.
cases.d: Bettina Janssen and Claudia Bundschuh presented their 140-page final report on the diocesan boarding school Albertinum in Gerolstein in February 2022, covering 1946 until it closed in 1983. Fifty-four former pupils came forward. Violence, mostly physical but including sexualised violence, was part of daily life; all three directors, who were priests, and one lay employee committed sexualised violence. Bishop Stephan Ackermann apologised and admitted the diocese had lacked effective oversight; the diocese later paid 650,000 euros to former pupils.
cases.cite: Bettina Janssen and Claudia Bundschuh, 'Gewalt am Bischöflichen Internat Albertinum Gerolstein', final report, February 2022 (epd via evangelisch.de, 12 February 2022)

cases.n: Korntal Brüdergemeinde children's homes — final report (2018)
cases.victims_note: 56 of 105 interviewees reported sexualised violence; 93 reported physical violence
cases.who: Evangelische Brüdergemeinde Korntal — three children's homes in Korntal and Wilhelmsdorf
cases.d: Retired judge Brigitte Baums-Stammberger and educational scientist Benno Hafeneger presented their 400-page report 'Uns wurde die Würde genommen' in Stuttgart on 7 June 2018, after 115 interviews with former residents. Of the 105 accounts used, 56 reported sexualised violence and 93 physical violence in three homes of the Protestant Brüdergemeinde in Korntal and Wilhelmsdorf from 1949 to the 1980s. A caretaker forced at least 30 children into sexual acts; a stable worker, a baker and a children's doctor were also named as serious offenders. The Brüdergemeinde apologised and paid recognition payments, usually 5,000 euros.
cases.cite: Brigitte Baums-Stammberger and Benno Hafeneger, final report on the Korntal children's homes, 7 June 2018 (epd via evangelisch.de)

cases.n: West German children's cure homes ('Verschickungskinder') — Humboldt University report (2025)
cases.victims_note: an estimated 11.4 million children stayed in cure and recreation homes 1951–1990; no count of abused children possible
cases.who: Children's cure homes run by welfare organisations, municipalities and private operators, financed by health and pension insurers; Deutsche Rentenversicherung, Caritas, Diakonie and German Red Cross
cases.d: A Humboldt University team led by historian Alexander Nützenadel published the first nationwide report on West German children's cure homes on 15 May 2025, jointly with the German pension insurance (DRV), Caritas, Diakonie and the German Red Cross. It estimates that 11.4 million children stayed in such homes between 1951 and 1990 and describes humiliation, intimidation and violence as structural, with inadequate supervision; press coverage reported that many children also suffered sexualised violence, though no count is possible. The four organisations expressed regret and accepted responsibility. An earlier North Rhine-Westphalia ministry study (January 2022) found over 2.1 million children sent from that state between 1949 and 1990.
cases.cite: Alexander Nützenadel et al., Humboldt-Universität zu Berlin, research report on children's cure homes 1945–1989, 15 May 2025 (Deutsche Rentenversicherung press release; epd, 19 May 2025)

cases.n: Bündnis 90/Die Grünen — review of paedophile advocacy in the party (2014–2016)
cases.victims_note: 12 victims of child sexual abuse contacted the party's working group; 3 received payments for abuse in the Emmaus community at Dachsberg, Kamp-Lintfort, in the early 1980s
cases.who: Bündnis 90/Die Grünen (federal party and Berlin branch); paedophile activist groups of the 1970s–80s
cases.d: The Göttingen Institute for Democracy Research led by Franz Walter, commissioned by the Greens, presented its report in November 2014: paedophile groups got demands to legalise sex between adults and children into several Green resolutions in the 1980s, until a clear break in 1989, while in the Berlin branch the debate continued into the mid-1990s. A Berlin state-party commission reported in May 2015. The party's working group, which ended in 2016, was contacted by 12 victims of child sexual abuse; three received payments for abuse in the Emmaus community at Dachsberg in Kamp-Lintfort in the early 1980s, where the party's co-responsibility could not be ruled out. The party apologised in 2014.
cases.cite: Bündnis 90/Die Grünen, 'Aufarbeitung und Verantwortung' (2016), summarising Franz Walter et al., Göttinger Institut für Demokratieforschung (2014) and the Berlin commission report (May 2015)

cases.n: Independent Commission (UKASK) study of paedosexual networks in Berlin (2021)
cases.who: Paedosexual networks in Berlin; supporters among scientists, the Greens, child-rights groups and parts of the left-liberal and autonomist scene; Berlin authorities
cases.cover: Authorities looked away for a long time and held victims partly responsible; in the 1960s–70s foster children were placed with paedosexual men, partly on the advice of educators.
cases.d: The federal Independent Commission for the Investigation of Child Sexual Abuse (UKASK) published a preliminary study by Iris Hax and Sven Reiß on 24 February 2021 on paedosexual networks in Berlin from the 1970s to the 2000s. It found that groups of men who sexually exploited boys used social movements and had support from scientists, for a time from the Greens, and from child-rights groups and parts of the left-liberal and autonomist scene, while the women's movement opposed them. Authorities looked away and partly blamed victims; boys were also commercially exploited around Bahnhof Zoo. The commission called for a nationwide investigation of such networks.
cases.cite: Iris Hax and Sven Reiß, preliminary study on paedosexual networks in Berlin, Unabhängige Kommission zur Aufarbeitung sexuellen Kindesmissbrauchs, 24 February 2021 (epd via evangelisch.de)

cases.n: Saarland University Hospital (UKS) — independent review commission (2023)
cases.victims_note: 52 confirmed of more than 80 suspected cases
cases.who: Universitätsklinikum des Saarlandes, Homburg — an assistant physician (died 2016) and hospital leadership
cases.cover: The hospital and prosecutors decided not to inform potentially affected families; relatives and the public learned of the suspicions only in 2019.
cases.d: An independent commission chaired by former BKA president Jörg Ziercke presented its final report on 24 May 2023 on suspected abuse at Saarland University Hospital. An assistant physician carried out medically unnecessary intimate examinations of children between 2010 and 2014; the hospital reported him at the end of 2014 and dismissed him, and the investigation ended when he died in 2016. The commission confirmed 52 of more than 80 suspected cases and found a lack of consistent leadership; the decision by the hospital and prosecutors not to inform families until 2019 was the main cause of lost trust. It recommended compensation of 5,000 to 50,000 euros per case.
cases.cite: Unabhängige Aufarbeitungskommission am Universitätsklinikum des Saarlandes, final report, 24 May 2023 (epd via evangelisch.de)

cases.n: Diocese of Rottenburg-Stuttgart — diocesan abuse figures (2023)
cases.who: Catholic Diocese of Rottenburg-Stuttgart — clergy, religious sisters and lay staff
cases.d: The Diocese of Rottenburg-Stuttgart's third report on investigation and recognition, dated 19 October 2023, counted 207 accused (114 priests, deacons and male religious with a diocesan contract, 17 other religious priests, 54 lay people and 21 religious sisters) and 421 known victims for 1946 to 2023. Cases are handled by the diocese's abuse commission (KsM), set up in 2002. The diocese's independent review commission published its first annual report in February 2023, and an IPP study covered the Josefsheim children's home in Ludwigsburg-Hoheneck.
cases.cite: Diözese Rottenburg-Stuttgart, 'Aufklärung, Aufarbeitung, Anerkennung des Leids', 3rd edition, 19 October 2023

cases.n: Tyrol and Vorarlberg — state-commissioned study of welfare and residential care (2015)
cases.victims_note: 362 people in Tyrol and 159 in Vorarlberg had received compensation since 2010
cases.who: State welfare system and residential homes of Tyrol and Vorarlberg, incl. Jagdberg (Schlins), St. Martin (Schwaz), Mariatal (Kramsach), Kleinvolderberg
cases.cover: The study found the institutional system produced, tolerated and failed to prevent physical, psychological and sexualised violence.
cases.d: A University of Innsbruck team led by Michaela Ralser, commissioned by the state governments of Tyrol and Vorarlberg, presented its overall study of welfare and residential care on 6 July 2015. It examined four state institutions in detail (Jagdberg, St. Martin, Mariatal and Kleinvolderberg) and found a total institution of isolation and dependence that produced, tolerated and did not prevent physical, psychological and sexualised violence until the 1980s. By then 362 people in Tyrol and 159 in Vorarlberg had received compensation from the states since 2010.
cases.cite: Michaela Ralser et al., 'Gesamtstudie zur Geschichte der Fürsorge- und Heimerziehung in Tirol und Vorarlberg', presented 6 July 2015 (Universität Innsbruck iPoint)

cases.n: Tyrol — 'Dreierkommission Martinsbühel' report on church-run children's homes (2022)
cases.who: Seven church-run children's homes in Tyrol (Martinsbühel, Scharnitz, Josefinum/Volders, Bubenburg/Fügen, St. Josef/Mils, Thurnfeld/Hall, Elisabethinum/Axams); Diocese of Innsbruck; Tyrolean youth welfare
cases.cover: Survivors said the state youth welfare office and school authorities looked too little; church and state officials acknowledged institutional responsibility.
cases.d: A commission set up in 2019 by the State of Tyrol, the Diocese of Innsbruck and religious orders, chaired by educational scientist Margret Aull, presented its final report 'Demut lernen' on 7 December 2022. Based on 75 interviews, it covered seven church-run children's homes in Tyrol after 1945, where former residents described sexualised and other violence; at Martinsbühel in the 1970s one sister supervised up to 50 girls. Survivors said state youth welfare and school authorities did not look closely enough. Diocesan leaders described the findings as 'total pedagogical failure' in church and state institutions.
cases.cite: Dreierkommission Martinsbühel, final report 'Demut lernen. Kindheit in konfessionellen Kinderheimen in Tirol nach 1945', 7 December 2022

cases.n: Vienna — historians' commission (2012) and Weisser Ring support programme for victims of city youth welfare (2010–2019)
cases.victims_note: 3,139 reports handled; 2,384 people received financial aid; sexual-abuse share not stated
cases.who: City of Vienna youth welfare — municipal, church and private children's homes and foster care, incl. the Kinderübernahmestelle (KÜST)
cases.d: A historians' commission led by Reinhard Sieder reported in May 2012 on Vienna's municipal, church and private children's homes after 1945, through which roughly 100,000 children passed; it described sadistic sexual abuse by some staff alongside widespread violence. The City of Vienna commissioned the victim-support organisation Weisser Ring in 2010 to handle claims of people harmed in Vienna youth welfare institutions between 1945 and 1999. Its final report (2019) records 3,139 reports and financial aid to 2,384 people, with 42.13 million euros paid directly to victims. The separate Wilhelminenberg commission is already on the map.
cases.cite: Reinhard Sieder et al., historians' commission on Vienna children's homes, May 2012 (profil, 21 May 2012); Weisser Ring, Abschlussbericht 'Hilfe für Opfer von Gewalt in Einrichtungen der Wiener Jugendwohlfahrt', 2019

cases.n: SOS Children's Villages — Independent Special Commission (ISC) worldwide report (2023)
cases.who: SOS Children's Villages (federation of member associations; International Senate); former senior staff
cases.cover: Former senior staff in some member associations knew of abuse and failed to act or concealed reports; serious abuse was not reported to national authorities.
cases.d: An Independent Special Commission appointed by the International Senate of SOS Children's Villages in 2021, chaired by former Kenyan Chief Justice Willy Mutunga with former Delhi High Court acting chief justice Gita Mittal, issued its summary report on 6 June 2023. Using a 'reasonable grounds to believe' standard, it confirmed serious allegations of child sexual and physical abuse in several member associations in Africa, Asia and Central America, and found cover-ups of past sexual abuse and failures to report to national authorities in more than one association. Countries named in the report include Nepal, Cambodia, India, Kenya, Panama, Sierra Leone and Syria. A confidential 991-page part two went to the organisation's leadership; Austrian prosecutors received parts of it in late 2025.
cases.cite: Independent Special Commission, Final Report Part One (Summary Report), SOS Children's Villages, 6 June 2023; Vorarlberg Online, 12 November 2025

cases.n: SOS-Kinderdorf Austria — abuse at Imst and Moosburg, founder Hermann Gmeiner, and the Griss reform commission (2025–2026)
cases.victims_note: 8 men abused as boys by founder Hermann Gmeiner at four villages (per SOS Austria, Oct 2025); an investigation report later listed 16 suspected cases against him
cases.who: SOS-Kinderdorf Österreich — children's villages incl. Imst (Tyrol) and Moosburg (Carinthia); founder Hermann Gmeiner (died 1986)
cases.cover: The allegations against Gmeiner were known internally for years (victims came forward 2013–2023) but were made public only in 2025.
cases.d: After a Falter report in September 2025 on abuse by staff at Austrian SOS children's villages, SOS-Kinderdorf Österreich said on 23 October 2025 that there were credible accounts that its founder Hermann Gmeiner sexually and physically abused eight boys at four villages between the 1950s and 1980s; victims had come forward from 2013 and received compensation, but the organisation had not made this public. A later investigation report listed 16 suspected cases of sexualised violence by Gmeiner. An external reform commission chaired by former Supreme Court president Irmgard Griss presented its results on 25 June 2026, focusing on abuse at Moosburg and Imst, handling of earlier studies and possible cover-ups, and the lack of external oversight. Prosecutors in Klagenfurt, Innsbruck and Salzburg opened investigations.
cases.cite: SOS-Kinderdorf Österreich statement (dpa via Blue News, 23 October 2025); Reformkommission (Irmgard Griss), results presented 25 June 2026 (ORF); investigation report on Gmeiner (stol.it, 26 June 2026)

cases.n: Diocese of Bolzano-Bressanone — Westpfahl Spilker Wastl report (2025)
cases.victims_note: 59 victims in proven or probable cases, 16 more unclear; 51% female
cases.who: Catholic Diocese of Bolzano-Bressanone (South Tyrol)
cases.cover: Handling of abuse cases until 2010 was a systemic failure; one priest was removed only in 2010 despite allegations from the 1960s.
cases.d: The Munich law firm Westpfahl Spilker Wastl, commissioned by the Diocese of Bolzano-Bressanone, published its report on 20 January 2025, the first such diocesan report in Italy, covering 1964 to 2023. It found 29 clerics against whom allegations were proven or highly probable, in 67 cases of sexual assault with 59 victims, plus 16 unclear cases; one priest abused girls as young as seven. It described the handling of cases until 2010 as a systemic failure. The bishop apologised.
cases.cite: Westpfahl Spilker Wastl (Wastl, Pusch, Gladstein, Schenke), report for the Diocese of Bolzano-Bressanone, January 2025 (Politiko via BishopAccountability.org, 21 January 2025)

cases.n: Italian Bishops' Conference (CEI) — national safeguarding reports (2022–2025)
cases.victims_note: 89 people in 2020–21 reports; 115 alleged victims in 2023–24; 613 clergy files sent to the Vatican 2000–2022
cases.who: Conferenza Episcopale Italiana — diocesan listening centres and the national child-protection service
cases.cover: Critics, including Rete l'Abuso, said the reports cover only recent diocesan-desk data and omit court and Vatican cases; the first report mentions no reports to civil authorities.
cases.d: The Italian Bishops' Conference published its first national report in November 2022, prepared with experts of the Università Cattolica: 80 diocesan listening centres had received 86 contacts in 2020–2021 concerning 89 people, against 68 alleged abusers, 44% of them clerics. CEI also said dioceses had sent 613 files on clerics to the Vatican's doctrine office since 2000. Its third survey, presented in May 2025, counted 115 alleged victims (64 boys, 51 girls) and 67 alleged perpetrators, 44 of them clergy, in 2023–2024. Critics said the reports are too narrow and Italy has no independent national inquiry.
cases.cite: CEI, 'Proteggere, prevenire, formare' first report, 17 November 2022 (Il Post); CEI Servizio Nazionale per la tutela dei minori, third territorial survey, 28 May 2025 (Sky TG24)

cases.n: Society of Jesus in Spain — report on abuse since 1927 (2021)
cases.victims_note: 81 minors and 37 adults (118 cases)
cases.who: Society of Jesus (Jesuits), Spain — 65 of the 96 accused abused children
cases.d: In January 2021 the Jesuits in Spain published a report admitting 118 cases of sexual abuse since 1927, 81 of them against children. It named 96 accused Jesuits, about 1.08% of members since 1927; of the 65 who abused children, 48 had died and 17 were alive. The order acknowledged that some accusations had not been adequately addressed. It was the first such report by a religious order in Spain.
cases.cite: Compañía de Jesús en España, report on abuse cases since 1927, January 2021 (JURIST, January 2021; AP)

cases.n: Marist Brothers in Spain — independent commission recognises 25 victims (2020)
cases.who: Marist Brothers (Hermanos Maristas) schools in Spain, incl. Barcelona
cases.d: On 3 December 2020 the Marist congregation in Spain announced that an independent commission it had set up to review all cases had recognised 25 victims of sexual abuse by former teachers in its schools, with compensation reported at about 400,000 euros in total, including for time-barred cases. The Barcelona cases, from 1970 to 2010, were exposed by local press in 2016. Only one teacher, lay PE teacher Joaquín Benítez, was tried; in 2019 he was sentenced to 21 years and nine months for abusing four pupils, other complaints being time-barred.
cases.cite: Hermanos Maristas, announcement of 3 December 2020 (EFE via Semanario Universidad)

cases.n: Catalonia — Síndic de Greuges (ombudsman) report on child sexual abuse in the Catholic Church (2020)
cases.who: Catholic religious congregations and dioceses in Catalonia
cases.cover: Congregations generally did not seek out other cases or offer reparation.
cases.d: A commission within the Catalan ombudsman's office (Síndic de Greuges), under Rafael Ribó, published its report on 2 October 2020. Most cases it heard concerned boys aged 5 to 17, abused repeatedly in the 1960s and 1970s on camps and excursions, on church premises and in abusers' flats, with three cases from the 1990s; documents pointed to many more victims than came forward. Religious congregations generally had not looked for other cases or offered reparation. Among seven recommendations, it asked the Catalan Parliament to create an inquiry commission, which the Parliament approved on 27 April 2022.
cases.cite: Síndic de Greuges de Catalunya, report on sexual abuse of children in the Catholic Church, 2 October 2020 (betevé)

cases.n: Mallorca — Consell de Mallorca commission on sexual exploitation of children in IMAS care (2021)
cases.victims_note: about 16 cases known in January 2020
cases.who: Institut Mallorquí d'Afers Socials (IMAS), the island's child-protection agency
cases.d: A commission of the Consell de Mallorca, chaired by vice-president Jaume Tortella, reported in April 2021 on the sexual exploitation of minors in the care of the island's child-protection agency IMAS, about 16 cases of which were known in January 2020, mostly from 2017 to early 2019. With the PP and Vox not taking part, it found no political, technical or criminal responsibility and no network linking the cases, matching the prosecutors' investigation. Reporting had changed in February 2020 so that suspicions go to the national police, and five cases not previously reported were sent to prosecutors. The opposition called for a separate inquiry, and an EU delegation visited Palma in April 2022.
cases.cite: Consell de Mallorca commission on minors in care, report presented 23 April 2021 (Ultima Hora)

cases.n: Belgian Chamber commission of inquiry on sexual abuse in the Church after 'Godvergeten' (2024)
cases.who: Catholic Church in Belgium; Belgian justice system
cases.cover: The commission noted 58% of cases are dismissed by prosecutors and called for a new inquiry into the 2010 'Operation Kelk' raids after the High Council of Justice reported dysfunctions.
cases.d: The federal Chamber set up a parliamentary commission of inquiry, chaired by Sophie De Wit (N-VA), after the 2023 VRT series 'Godvergeten' on abuse in the Catholic Church. Its report of 2 May 2024 made 137 recommendations, including that the Church acknowledge responsibility, trace perpetrators in its archives and open files to police and courts, and a study on retroactively ending the limitation period. It noted that 58% of abuse cases are dismissed by prosecutors and asked for a new inquiry into the 2010 'Operation Kelk' investigation. It proposed an abuse commissioner, a centre of expertise and an arbitration body for time-barred cases.
cases.cite: Chamber of Representatives, special commission of inquiry on sexual abuse in the Church and elsewhere, report of 2 May 2024 (VRT NWS)

cases.n: Deetman Commission — supplementary inquiry into abuse of and violence against girls in the Catholic Church (2013)
cases.victims_note: 79 new reports, 37 of them without sexual abuse; 26 earlier reports from women reconsidered
cases.who: Roman Catholic Church in the Netherlands — dioceses and religious orders
cases.d: The Deetman Commission presented a supplementary inquiry on 11 March 2013 into sexual abuse of and violence against girls and young women who were minors in the Dutch Catholic Church from 1945 to 2012, after its 2011 report had found over 77% of identified victims were male. It received 79 new reports, of which 37 concerned only physical or psychological violence, and reconsidered 71 earlier reports of violence, 26 from women. It called on bishops and religious superiors to reach out to these victims; reports involving sexual abuse go to the Church's reporting point and compensation committees.
cases.cite: Commissie-Deetman, aanvullend onderzoek 'Seksueel misbruik van en geweld tegen meisjes in de Rooms-Katholieke Kerk', 11 March 2013 (rkkerk.nl)

cases.n: Territorial Abbey of Saint-Maurice — independent working group report (2025)
cases.who: Abbey of Saint-Maurice (canons regular) and its boarding school, Valais
cases.d: An independent working group formed at the request of the abbey, then under a Vatican-appointed apostolic administrator, by Neuchâtel attorney general Pierre Aubert presented its findings on 20 June 2025. Historians of the University of Fribourg (Anne-Françoise Praz, Stéphanie Roulin and others) and retired judge Claire-Lise Mayor Aubert examined sexual violence at the abbey and its boarding school from 1960 to 2024, how the institution handled cases, how victims were heard and what happened to perpetrators. The mandate did not cover the abbey's collège. The report made recommendations to the abbey.
cases.cite: Groupe de travail indépendant (Université de Fribourg), 'Violences sexuelles à l'Abbaye de Saint-Maurice 1960–2024', 20 June 2025

cases.n: Malta — Church Response Team figures on clergy abuse 1991–2010
cases.victims_note: 45 cases of abuse involving minors (not a victim count)
cases.who: Catholic Church in Malta — Response Team set up by the Maltese bishops (chair Judge Victor Caruana Colombo)
cases.d: In April 2010 the Maltese Curia said the Church's Response Team, set up by the bishops in 1991 and chaired by Judge Victor Caruana Colombo, had handled 45 cases of abuse of minors by priests over 19 years. Nineteen were dismissed as unfounded, 13 remained open, four priests were found guilty and removed from ministry, and two priests had died. The convictions over St Joseph Home are already on the map.
cases.cite: Archdiocese of Malta, statement on the Response Team, 13 April 2010 (Blitz Quotidiano)

cases.n: Slovakia — bishops' commission evaluation report on abuse 2018–2023 (2024)
cases.victims_note: more than 44 victims in 39 confirmed cases; likely higher
cases.who: Catholic Church in Slovakia — Latin dioceses, Greek Catholic eparchies and religious orders
cases.d: The Slovak bishops' commission for the protection of minors published its 'Evaluation Report 2018–2023' in March 2024, the first such report in Slovakia, counting complaints from 1990 onward. Of 68 complaints, 39 were confirmed and closed, 17 remained open, 7 could not be resolved and 5 were not confirmed; the confirmed cases involved more than 44 victims. Fifty complaints concerned Latin-rite dioceses, three Greek Catholic eparchies and 15 religious orders.
cases.cite: Slovak Bishops' Conference, commission for the protection of minors, 'Evaluation Report 2018–2023', March 2024 (The Pillar via BishopAccountability.org, 6 March 2024)

cases.n: Latvia — Logos Centrs child exploitation network, Riga (1999–2002 convictions)
cases.victims_note: 67 people sexually exploited, 61 of them minors; the agency had catalogued about 3,000 minors
cases.who: Logos Centrs video and model agency, Riga (director Jurijs Jurjevs)
cases.d: In 1999 Latvian investigators found that the Riga agency Logos Centrs, headed by psychiatrist Jurijs Jurjevs, had sexually exploited 67 people, 61 of them minors, and produced abuse material; it had catalogued about 3,000 minors. Jurjevs was sentenced to more than four years; Andris Meinarts was convicted on 21 counts and sentenced to ten years; former 'Miss Latvia' manager Ainārs Eisaks received 2.5 years for abusing minors; Ingus Tūns received five years in a separate case. Claims that senior politicians were clients were investigated and rejected (see the Saeima commission record).
cases.cite: Wikipedia, 'Logos Centrs pedophilia case', citing Latvijas Vēstnesis (2000), The Guardian (2000), Delfi and The Baltic Times

cases.n: Latvia — Saeima paedophilia commission's claims against senior officials (2000), found false
cases.who: Saeima investigation commission chaired by MP Jānis Ādamsons; former PM Andris Šķēle, ex-justice minister Valdis Birkavs, State Revenue Service head Andrejs Sončiks (accused, cleared)
cases.d: After a September 1999 TV report on the Logos Centrs case, the Saeima set up an investigation commission chaired by opposition MP Jānis Ādamsons, who in February 2000 publicly linked former prime minister Andris Šķēle, former justice minister Valdis Birkavs and revenue service head Andrejs Sončiks to the paedophilia case. On 1 August 2000 the Prosecutor General's Office closed the case, stating it was 'fully proved' that the information given to the commission was false and that no crime had been committed. Ādamsons was later convicted of abuse of office for knowingly spreading false information and fined. None of the officials was charged.
cases.cite: Prosecutor General's Office of Latvia, decision of 1 August 2000 (The Baltic Times, 3 August 2000); Wikipedia, 'Logos Centrs pedophilia case'

notes:
EUROPE PART 2 (follow-up to expand_europe.json). Worked through every candidate in expand_europe.json's notes, then re-checked the listed small and eastern countries. Main finding aids opened: the KNA overview of German diocesan studies (Vatican News, Jan 2022), the German Bishops' Conference overview of published reappraisal reports (29 May 2024), and the Independent Commission's (UKASK) bibliography of reappraisal reports (May 2026). Records cite the reports or major outlets, not the aids. Note that bishop-accountability.org list pages could not be opened directly (blocked as not previously seen); individual pages found by search were opened.

BORDERLINE CALLS (same conventions as expand_europe.json): (1) Whole-diocese studies count as 'whole region'. (2) Whole-institution reports on a single school or home were added when the study covers the whole institution and was commissioned by the operator or a church body (Aloisiuskolleg, Josephinum, Albertinum, Korntal, Saarland UKS, Saint-Maurice), following the earlier agent's Ettal/Kremsmünster precedent; they are small (54-100 accounts) and the caller may prefer to keep them as map cases only. (3) National church or order self-counts were added as 'acknowledged' like the Polish 2019 figures (CEI Italy, Malta, Slovakia, Spanish Jesuits); a single diocese's self-count (Rottenburg-Stuttgart) was excluded from the checklist but kept as a case, matching the Luxembourg exclusion. (4) The Greens' review and the UKASK Berlin networks study are included as organised-network findings; the Greens item has few documented victims. (5) The Mallorca commission is an island-government body (counted as regional) and found no network and no responsibility. (6) The Latvian Saeima commission is listed because its claims about officials were officially found false (status 'disproved'); the underlying Logos Centrs network convictions are added as a separate case (not a checklist item: 61 minors). (7) The Verschickungskinder report is a national self-study by the pension insurance and three welfare federations; the press release does not mention sexualised violence, the epd report does, and no number is given.

UPDATES FOR RECORDS IN expand_europe.json (not edited here): x-deu-osnabrueck-study-2022 — the University of Osnabrück final study was presented on 2 October 2024 (1945 to present): 122 accused priests and deacons and more than 400 victims (Vatican News, 9 Oct 2024: https://www.vaticannews.va/de/kirche/news/2024-10/katholische-kirche-missbrauch-deutschland-bistum-osnabrueck.html). aut-groer-klasnic: the earlier agent's note on the Klasnic figures (2,550 approved cases to Aug 2021) was not re-checked.

FOLDED INTO OTHER RECORDS: Speyer Engelsgasse children's home (Niederbronn Sisters; social-court compensation 2020) is described inside x-deu-speyer-schraut-2025. Hildesheim IPP 2017 is inside x-deu-hildesheim-2021. Würzburg file reviews 2019 and the Kilianeen study are inside x-deu-wuerzburg-schneider-2025. Augsburg's two children's-home studies (Heilig Kreuz Donauwörth, Reitenbuch) are mentioned in x-deu-augsburg-uaka-2025. Limburg annual reports (2024 onward) folded into x-deu-limburg-2020. Vienna Heimopfer programme and Sieder historians' commission combined in one record. Malta's later Safeguarding Commission annual figures (e.g. 12 cases in one year) folded into x-mlt-response-team-2010. Polish Episcopate follow-up statistics (ISKK, 2021) belong to pol-episcopate-2019-sekielski.

COULD NOT CONFIRM (no source opened that states the finding; NOT on the checklist):
- Germany: Joint commission of the Hamburg metropolis (UAK Nord: Hamburg, Hildesheim, Osnabrück) — only interim reports 2024 and 2024/25 are listed; figures not found. Bamberg, Dresden-Meißen, Görlitz, Magdeburg: no diocesan study published per the DBK list (May 2024). Regensburg diocese beyond the Domspatzen: no diocese-wide study per KNA 2022. Rottenburg-Stuttgart independent commission annual reports (2023, 2024): figures not read. EKHN (Hesse-Nassau) children's homes study 2018 (Neff et al.): listed by UKASK, content not found. GDR residential care study 2023 (Gahleitner et al., 'Sexualisierte Gewalt in der Heimerziehung der DDR'): listed, content not opened; may belong with x-deu-ukask-gdr-2019. Berlin State Ballet School commission (2020) and Sternsinger/Kindermissionswerk report on Winfried Pilz (2023, single offender): not opened. Christusträger excluded (above).
- Austria: Salzburg state and university study on violence against children in homes and foster care after 1945 (plus.ac.at PDF) not opened; Klasnic update not re-checked.
- Spain: Catalan Parliament commission of inquiry (approved 27 April 2022) — no published conclusions found; the legislature ended early in 2024. Diocese of Cartagena inquiry (announced 2020) not searched. CONFER/other orders' counts (rr.pt: 'religious orders admit 126 cases', Feb 2021) not opened.
- Netherlands: KNGU gymnastics inquiry (2021) not opened (earlier agent: mainly non-sexual).
- Belgium: church annual reports (e.g. 2023) not re-checked; Flemish Parliament resolution on church abuse (Brussels Times) not opened.
- Switzerland: Reformed Church (EKS) national study was halted before starting (SRF headline 'Stopp für Missbrauchsstudie'); University of Zurich follow-up study (2024–2026) results not found yet; Einsiedeln — only an abbot's internal investigation reported (Beobachter).
- Poland: State Commission reports after 2022 (third and later) not found in searches; Jesuit and Kraków archdiocese reports not found; the planned Church-appointed independent commission was not set up (Rzeczpospolita: 'only in 2024'; later the primate declined to set it up); '1,000+ victims of clergy in communist Poland (2023)' — body not identified.
- Holy See: no new items beyond those on the map.
- SOS Children's Villages: SOS-Kinderdorf Austria's own earlier studies and the full ISC Part Two are confidential; abuse counts per country were not published in the summary.

COUNTRY RE-CHECK (official in-scope findings): Slovakia — added (bishops' report 2024). Latvia — added (Saeima commission, disproved; Logos Centrs convictions). Liechtenstein — none found. Cyprus — the Commissioner for Children's 2022 report on children in state care (90 complaints 2011–2021) does not mention sexual abuse in the coverage opened; none found. Greece — no official finding: the 'Ark of the World' charity case (Fr Antonios Papanikolaou) was before Athens courts in 2024 on physical-abuse charges with separate felony sexual-abuse charges pending; a 2021 Athens orphanage investigation is press-reported only. Czechia — no national study; survivors' petitions for an investigation (Radio Prague) only; Fr Merta conviction already on map. Bulgaria — ECtHR X and Others v. Bulgaria (2021) excluded (above); Ombudsman NPM reports address violence in boarding schools generally. Moldova — the children's ombudswoman referred single cases (e.g. a summer camp) to prosecutors; no institution-wide finding. Belarus, Estonia, Russia — none found (not separately searched beyond the general sweeps; documentation is thin).
